corrections.original: When I travel, now use a hair dryer at the hotel, instead of just towel dry my hair.
corrections.selfCorrectionCue: Put 'now' after the subject, and use -ing after 'instead of.'
corrections.natural: When I travel, I now use a hair dryer at the hotel instead of just towel-drying my hair.
corrections.reason: The adverb naturally follows the subject, and 'instead of' is followed by a noun or gerund.

corrections.original: I want to change the morning commute, because it's tiring.
corrections.selfCorrectionCue: Whose commute is it? Use the possessive form.
corrections.natural: I want to change my morning commute because it's tiring.
corrections.reason: Use 'my morning commute' for your own routine, and no comma is needed before this short 'because' clause.

corrections.original: Whether it is raining, it is really getting hot. You know, the autumn is coming Then ... It's easier to go more than now.
corrections.selfCorrectionCue: Use 'even when' for contrast, then make one clear future prediction.
corrections.natural: The weather has been really hot, even when it rains. It might get easier when the weather cools down in autumn.
corrections.reason: 'Whether' introduces alternatives, while 'even when' expresses the contrast you meant. 'Get easier' is more natural than 'go more than now.'

lessonNote.finalVersion: When I travel, I now use a hair dryer at the hotel instead of just towel-drying my hair. Another routine I would like to improve is my morning commute. I usually take a bus, but I also have to walk part of the way, and that can be tiring. The weather makes it harder because it has been very hot, even on rainy days. I think the commute may feel much easier when the weather cools down in autumn.
